about: Thermodynamics and Heat Transfer (AERO40009) is a core 5-credit Year 1 module on Imperial's MEng Aeronautical Engineering, taught in the Spring term according to the 2026-27 programme specification. The same programme has a Year 2 core module, Propulsion and Turbomachinery (AERO50009), that uses this material. Imperial's detailed module descriptor could not be opened for this pack, so the topics follow a standard first course built from the module's title and its place in the programme: definitions, the first and second laws, introductory gas dynamics, conduction, convection, radiation, and problems that combine them. No module-specific assessment breakdown was found; the programme specification gives only a Year 1 average of roughly 71% examination, 20% coursework and 9% practical.
topics: The first law and the steady-flow energy equation
The second law, entropy and component efficiency

notes.h: Systems, properties and the perfect gas
notes.body:
Aeronautical thermodynamics deals mostly with air and combustion gases flowing through intakes, compressors, combustors, turbines and nozzles. Before using any law, you need a clear vocabulary.

Systems and control volumes
- A closed system is a fixed mass. Heat and work cross its boundary, but mass does not.
- A control volume is a fixed region that fluid flows through, such as a jet-engine compressor or a nozzle. Most propulsion problems use control volumes.
- An isolated system exchanges neither mass nor energy with its surroundings.

Properties, state and processes
- Properties describe the state: pressure p, temperature T, density ρ (or specific volume v = 1/ρ), internal energy u, enthalpy h and entropy s.
- Intensive properties (p, T, ρ) do not depend on the amount of matter. Extensive properties (V, U, H) do; per unit mass they become specific properties (u, h, s).
- For a single-phase gas, two independent intensive properties fix the state.
- Heat and work are not properties. They are energy in transit across a boundary, and their amounts depend on the path (they are path functions).
- A quasi-static process passes through a series of equilibrium states. A cycle returns to its starting state.
- The zeroth law (two bodies each in thermal equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other) makes temperature measurement meaningful.

The perfect (ideal) gas
- Equation of state: p = ρRT, or pv = RT, with R = R̄/M. For air, R ≈ 287 J/(kg K).
- A calorically perfect gas has constant specific heats: c_p ≈ 1005 J/(kg K), c_v ≈ 718 J/(kg K) and γ = c_p/c_v ≈ 1.4 for air near room temperature.
- Relations: c_p − c_v = R, c_p = γR/(γ − 1), c_v = R/(γ − 1).
- For a perfect gas u and h depend on T only: Δu = c_v ΔT and Δh = c_p ΔT.
- At high temperatures, such as in a combustor, c_p rises and γ falls, so constant-property results are approximations.

Units and conventions
- Use absolute temperature (K) and absolute pressure (Pa) in every equation.
- 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa. In the International Standard Atmosphere, sea level is at 101 325 Pa and 288.15 K.
- Example: at ISA sea level, ρ = p/(RT) = 101 325/(287 × 288.15) ≈ 1.225 kg/m³.

Stagnation (total) properties
- For flowing gas, the stagnation state is the state reached by bringing the flow to rest adiabatically. With no work, the stagnation enthalpy is h₀ = h + V²/2 and the stagnation temperature is T₀ = T + V²/(2c_p).
- If the deceleration is also reversible (isentropic), the stagnation pressure is p₀ = p(T₀/T)^(γ/(γ−1)).
- These ideas link thermodynamics with aerodynamics and propulsion, and they appear in every later topic.

Exam tips: state your system or control volume, your assumptions (perfect gas, steady flow, adiabatic) and the property values you use. Most numerical errors come from using °C, gauge pressure or c_v where c_p is needed.

notes.h: First law for closed systems and steady flow
notes.body:
The first law is conservation of energy. In aeronautics it is used mostly in its steady-flow form, applied to each engine component in turn.

Closed system
- With Q as heat added and W as work done by the system: Q − W = ΔU (+ ΔKE + ΔPE).
- Quasi-static boundary work is W = ∫p dV. For a polytropic process pVⁿ = constant (n ≠ 1), W = (p₂V₂ − p₁V₁)/(1 − n).
- Over a cycle, ΔU = 0, so net heat in equals net work out.
- Some courses count work done on the system as positive, which turns the law into Q + W = ΔU. Use your lecture-note convention and state it.

Steady-flow energy equation (SFEE)
- For a control volume with one inlet and one outlet, in steady flow: Q̇ − Ẇ_x = ṁ[(h₂ + V₂²/2 + gz₂) − (h₁ + V₁²/2 + gz₁)], where Ẇ_x is shaft power out.
- Enthalpy appears because the flow work pv needed to push fluid in and out is combined with u.
- Using stagnation enthalpy h₀ = h + V²/2 and neglecting gravity, the SFEE becomes q − w_x = h₀₂ − h₀₁.

Applying it to gas-turbine components (perfect gas, c_p constant)
- Intake or diffuser: adiabatic, no work, so h₀ is constant. T₀ is unchanged while V falls and T rises.
- Compressor: adiabatic, so w_in = c_p(T₀₂ − T₀₁).
- Combustor: no work, q = c_p(T₀₂ − T₀₁). This is an approximation, because composition and c_p change.
- Turbine: adiabatic, so w_out = c_p(T₀₁ − T₀₂).
- Nozzle: adiabatic, no work, so T₀ is constant, and the exit velocity is V = √(2c_p(T₀ − T)).

Mass conservation
- ṁ = ρAV is constant along a steady stream tube.

Worked example (compressor): air enters at T₀₁ = 288 K and is compressed through a stagnation pressure ratio of 10 with an isentropic efficiency of 0.85.
- Isentropic exit: T₀₂s = 288 × 10^(0.4/1.4) ≈ 556.0 K.
- Actual exit: T₀₂ = 288 + (556.0 − 288)/0.85 ≈ 603.3 K.
- Work input: w = 1.005 × 315.3 ≈ 317 kJ/kg.

Worked example (stagnation temperature): flight at 250 m/s in air at 220 K gives T₀ = 220 + 250²/2010 ≈ 251 K. This is why the leading edges and pitot probes of fast aircraft run warmer than the surrounding air.

Units: if c_p is in kJ/(kg K), V²/2 must be divided by 1000 so the units match.

Exam tips: always list the SFEE terms you are dropping and why. Use stagnation quantities for components with significant velocities, and check that the signs of q and w match your convention.

notes.h: Second law, entropy and isentropic efficiency
notes.body:
The first law allows any energy conversion that balances. The second law says which ones can actually happen, and it gives the ideal standard against which compressors, turbines, intakes and nozzles are judged.

Statements of the second law
- Kelvin–Planck: no cyclic device can turn heat from a single reservoir entirely into work.
- Clausius: heat cannot pass on its own from a colder body to a hotter one. A refrigerator needs work input.
- The Carnot efficiency, η = 1 − T_L/T_H (kelvin), is the upper limit for any engine working between two reservoirs.

Entropy
- Entropy is defined by dS = δQ_rev/T. For any real process, ΔS = ∫δQ/T + S_gen with S_gen ≥ 0. S_gen is zero only for a reversible process.
- For an isolated system, entropy never decreases.
- Gibbs relations: T ds = du + p dv = dh − v dp.
- Perfect gas: s₂ − s₁ = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁).
- Using stagnation values: s₂ − s₁ = c_p ln(T₀₂/T₀₁) − R ln(p₀₂/p₀₁). In an adiabatic duct with T₀ constant, any entropy rise appears as a loss of stagnation pressure: p₀₂/p₀₁ = exp(−Δs/R). This is why losses in intakes and across shock waves are quoted as stagnation-pressure losses.

Isentropic processes
- Adiabatic plus reversible means isentropic. For a perfect gas this gives T₂/T₁ = (p₂/p₁)^((γ−1)/γ), and pv^γ = constant.
- On a T–s diagram, lines of constant pressure slope upward and spread apart as s increases. An isentropic process is a vertical line.

Component efficiencies (same inlet state, same exit pressure)
- Compressor: η_c = (T₀₂s − T₀₁)/(T₀₂ − T₀₁), which is ideal work ÷ actual work.
- Turbine: η_t = (T₀₁ − T₀₂)/(T₀₁ − T₀₂s), which is actual work ÷ ideal work.
- Both are below 1. The actual compressor exit is hotter than the isentropic one, and the actual turbine exit is also hotter than the isentropic one.

Worked example (turbine): gas at 1400 K expands through a pressure ratio of 8 (γ = 1.4).
- T₂s = 1400 × (1/8)^0.2857 ≈ 772.9 K.
- If the actual exit temperature is 850 K, then η_t = (1400 − 850)/(1400 − 772.9) ≈ 0.877.

Worked example (heating): heating air at constant pressure from 300 K to 600 K gives Δs = 1.005 ln 2 ≈ 0.697 kJ/(kg K).

Why it matters for propulsion
- Brayton (Joule) cycle efficiency rises with pressure ratio: η = 1 − 1/r_p^((γ−1)/γ) for the ideal cycle.
- Component inefficiencies and stagnation-pressure losses lower the cycle's net work. This is studied further in later propulsion modules.

Exam tips: be clear whether you are using static or stagnation temperatures, and never confuse adiabatic with isentropic. A process can be adiabatic and still generate entropy.

notes.h: Compressible flow: Mach number, isentropic relations, choking and shocks
notes.body:
Once flow speeds are a significant fraction of the speed of sound, density changes matter, and thermodynamics and fluid mechanics combine into gas dynamics. This topic underpins intakes, nozzles and high-speed aerodynamics.

Speed of sound and Mach number
- Small pressure waves travel at a = √(γRT) in a perfect gas. At 288.15 K this is about 340 m/s, and at 216.65 K (the ISA tropopause) it is about 295 m/s.
- Mach number: M = V/a. Flow is subsonic for M < 1, sonic at M = 1 and supersonic for M > 1. Compressibility effects become important above roughly M ≈ 0.3.

Isentropic stagnation relations (perfect gas)
- T₀/T = 1 + ((γ − 1)/2)M².
- p₀/p = (T₀/T)^(γ/(γ−1)).
- ρ₀/ρ = (T₀/T)^(1/(γ−1)).
- For air (γ = 1.4), T₀/T = 1 + 0.2M² and p₀/p = (1 + 0.2M²)^3.5.
- Example: at M = 0.8 and 216.65 K, T₀ ≈ 244.4 K and p₀/p ≈ 1.524.

Critical (sonic) conditions
- At M = 1, T*/T₀ = 2/(γ + 1), which is 0.833 for air.
- p*/p₀ = (2/(γ + 1))^(γ/(γ−1)), which is 0.528 for air.
- ρ*/ρ₀ = (2/(γ + 1))^(1/(γ−1)), which is 0.634 for air.

Area–velocity behaviour
- In steady isentropic flow, dA/A = (M² − 1) dV/V.
- Subsonic flow speeds up in a converging duct. Supersonic flow speeds up in a diverging duct.
- So M = 1 can only occur at a throat, and reaching supersonic speed needs a convergent–divergent (de Laval) nozzle.
- Area–Mach relation: A/A* = (1/M)[(2/(γ+1))(1 + ((γ−1)/2)M²)]^((γ+1)/(2(γ−1))). For air at M = 2, A/A* ≈ 1.688.

Choking
- In a convergent nozzle fed from a reservoir, lowering the back pressure increases the flow until the throat reaches M = 1. This happens when the back pressure is at or below about 0.528p₀ for air.
- After that, the mass flow cannot increase further. It is fixed by ṁ = A* p₀ √(γ/(RT₀)) (2/(γ+1))^((γ+1)/(2(γ−1))), which for air is about 0.0404 A* p₀/√T₀ (SI units).
- Example: with p₀ = 5 bar, T₀ = 500 K and A* = 0.01 m², the choked flow is about 9.04 kg/s.

Normal shock waves
- A normal shock is a very thin, irreversible jump from supersonic to subsonic flow. T₀ is unchanged (adiabatic), but entropy rises, so p₀ falls.
- For γ = 1.4 and upstream M₁ = 2: M₂ ≈ 0.577, p₂/p₁ = 4.5, T₂/T₁ ≈ 1.69 and p₀₂/p₀₁ ≈ 0.721.
- Useful relations: p₂/p₁ = 1 + (2γ/(γ+1))(M₁² − 1) and M₂² = [1 + ((γ−1)/2)M₁²]/[γM₁² − (γ−1)/2].

Exam tips: decide first whether the flow is choked by comparing the back pressure with 0.528p₀. Use stagnation quantities as your reference, and remember that T₀ stays constant across a shock while p₀ does not.

notes.h: Conduction: Fourier's law and thermal resistance
notes.body:
Heat transfer is about rates: how fast energy moves because of a temperature difference. Thermodynamics tells you how much energy is involved, and heat transfer tells you how long it takes. Conduction is energy transfer through a material by molecular activity, without bulk motion.

Fourier's law
- In one dimension: q″ = −k dT/dx, where q″ is the heat flux (W/m²) and k is the thermal conductivity (W/(m K)).
- The minus sign shows that heat flows down the temperature gradient.
- Typical k values: metals are high (copper about 400, aluminium about 200 W/(m K)), gases are low (air about 0.026 W/(m K)), and insulating foams and fibres are very low because they trap gas.

Steady one-dimensional plane wall (no heat generation)
- The temperature profile is linear, and the heat rate is Q̇ = kA(T₁ − T₂)/L.
- Thermal resistance: R_cond = L/(kA), so Q̇ = ΔT/R, just like Ohm's law with ΔT as voltage and Q̇ as current.
- Example: a 0.2 m brick wall (k = 0.7 W/(m K)) of area 10 m² with a 20 K difference across it conducts Q̇ = 0.7 × 10 × 20/0.2 = 700 W.

Composite walls
- Layers in series: add their resistances, R_total = Σ Lᵢ/(kᵢA). The same Q̇ passes through each layer.
- Paths in parallel: add their conductances (1/R).
- Convection at a surface acts as a resistance 1/(hA) in series with the conduction resistances.
- Contact resistance at imperfect joints can be added as another series term.

Cylinders (pipes, insulated ducts)
- For a cylindrical shell from r₁ to r₂, length L: R_cyl = ln(r₂/r₁)/(2πkL).
- The temperature profile is logarithmic, not linear.
- For a spherical shell: R_sph = (1/r₁ − 1/r₂)/(4πk).

The heat diffusion equation
- In general, ρc ∂T/∂t = ∇·(k∇T) + q̇_gen. For steady 1D conduction with constant k and no generation, d²T/dx² = 0, which gives the linear profile.
- Thermal diffusivity α = k/(ρc) controls how quickly temperature changes spread through a solid.

Aerospace relevance
- Engine casings, cabin walls and thermal protection systems are designed as layered walls.
- A low-conductivity layer, such as an insulation blanket or a thermal barrier coating on turbine blades, carries most of the temperature drop.

Exam tips: draw the resistance network before calculating anything. Check that the temperature drops across the layers are in proportion to their resistances, and use the logarithmic resistance for any curved wall.

notes.h: Convection: heat transfer coefficients and dimensionless groups
notes.body:
Convection is heat transfer between a surface and a moving fluid. It combines conduction in the fluid right next to the wall with energy carried away by the flow. It is essential for cooling turbine blades, avionics and engine oil, and for predicting the heating of high-speed surfaces.

Newton's law of cooling
- q″ = h(T_s − T∞), where h is the convective heat transfer coefficient (W/(m² K)).
- h is not a material property. It depends on the flow velocity, the fluid properties, the geometry and whether the boundary layer is laminar or turbulent.
- Rough ranges: free convection in gases about 2–25; forced convection in gases about 25–250; forced convection in liquids about 100–20 000; boiling and condensation higher still (W/(m² K)).

Forced and natural convection
- In forced convection, an external device or the vehicle's own motion drives the flow.
- In natural (free) convection, buoyancy from density differences drives the flow. It is governed by the Grashof number Gr = gβΔTL³/ν², or by the Rayleigh number Ra = Gr·Pr.

Dimensionless groups
- Reynolds number: Re = ρVL/μ = VL/ν, the ratio of inertial to viscous forces. It decides whether the flow is laminar or turbulent.
- Prandtl number: Pr = ν/α = c_pμ/k, the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. It is about 0.7 for air and roughly 5–7 for water near room temperature.
- Nusselt number: Nu = hL/k_f, where k_f is the conductivity of the fluid. It is the dimensionless heat transfer coefficient.
- Correlations take the form Nu = f(Re, Pr) for forced convection and Nu = f(Gr, Pr) for natural convection.

Boundary layers
- A velocity boundary layer and a thermal boundary layer grow along a surface. Their relative thickness depends on Pr.
- h is highest where the boundary layer is thinnest, at the leading edge, and it rises sharply when the flow becomes turbulent.
- On a flat plate, transition usually occurs at Re_x of about 5 × 10⁵.

Standard correlations (check the conditions of use)
- Laminar flat plate, constant wall temperature, Pr ≳ 0.6: local Nu_x = 0.332 Re_x^(1/2) Pr^(1/3); average over length L, Nu_L = 0.664 Re_L^(1/2) Pr^(1/3).
- Fully developed turbulent pipe flow (Dittus–Boelter): Nu_D = 0.023 Re_D^0.8 Pr^n, with n = 0.4 when the fluid is heated and n = 0.3 when it is cooled.

Worked example: air at 5 m/s flows along a 0.5 m plate (ν = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s, k = 0.026 W/(m K), Pr = 0.71).
- Re_L = 5 × 0.5/1.6 × 10⁻⁵ ≈ 1.56 × 10⁵, which is laminar.
- Nu_L = 0.664 × 395.3 × 0.892 ≈ 234.
- h = Nu k/L ≈ 234 × 0.026/0.5 ≈ 12.2 W/(m² K).

High-speed flow
- At high Mach number, friction heats the gas near the wall. Convective heating is then driven by the difference between the adiabatic wall (recovery) temperature, which is close to T₀, and the wall temperature, not by T∞. Later modules treat this properly.

Exam tips: work out Re first to choose a laminar or turbulent correlation, use the fluid's k (not the solid's) in Nu, and state whether you are using a local or an average value.

notes.h: Thermal radiation: black and grey bodies
notes.body:
Every surface above absolute zero emits electromagnetic radiation. Unlike conduction and convection, radiation needs no medium, so it is the only way a spacecraft can reject heat. It also matters for combustor liners, turbine blades and the thermal protection of re-entry vehicles.

Black bodies
- A black body absorbs all incident radiation and, at a given temperature, emits the most energy possible.
- Stefan–Boltzmann law: E_b = σT⁴, with σ ≈ 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/(m² K⁴) and T in kelvin.
- Wien's displacement law: λ_max T ≈ 2898 µm K. A body at 5800 K, roughly the Sun's surface, peaks near 0.5 µm (visible light). A surface at 300 K peaks near 10 µm (infrared).

Real surfaces
- Emissivity: ε = E/E_b, between 0 and 1.
- Absorptivity α, reflectivity ρ and transmissivity τ satisfy α + ρ + τ = 1. For an opaque body τ = 0.
- Kirchhoff's law: for a surface in thermal equilibrium with its surroundings, α_λ = ε_λ at each wavelength. A grey surface has properties independent of wavelength, so α = ε.
- Polished metals have low ε. Oxidised metals, paints and many non-metals have high ε. Spacecraft radiators use coatings with low solar absorptivity but high infrared emissivity, which works because α and ε can differ across different wavelength bands.

Exchange between surfaces
- Small grey body in large surroundings: Q̇ = εσA(T_s⁴ − T_sur⁴).
- View factor F_ij is the fraction of radiation leaving surface i that strikes surface j. Reciprocity: A_iF_ij = A_jF_ji. Summation: ΣF_ij = 1 for an enclosure.
- Two infinite parallel grey plates: q″ = σ(T₁⁴ − T₂⁴)/(1/ε₁ + 1/ε₂ − 1).
- Radiation shields, such as thin low-emissivity foils between surfaces, greatly reduce exchange. This is the idea behind multi-layer insulation.

Linearised radiation coefficient
- For combining with convection: Q̇ = h_rA(T_s − T_sur), where h_r = εσ(T_s + T_sur)(T_s² + T_sur²).

Worked example: a pipe surface at 400 K with ε = 0.8 sits in a large room at 300 K.
- q″ = 0.8 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × (400⁴ − 300⁴) ≈ 794 W/m².
- h_r ≈ 7.9 W/(m² K), which is comparable to free convection. That is why radiation can rarely be ignored at modest temperatures.

Worked example: parallel plates at 600 K and 400 K, both with ε = 0.8.
- q″ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × (600⁴ − 400⁴)/1.5 ≈ 3.93 kW/m², against about 5.90 kW/m² for black plates.

Exam tips: always use kelvin (T⁴ makes Celsius errors huge), check which exchange formula matches the geometry, and state the grey and diffuse assumptions.

notes.h: Combined modes: resistance networks, insulation and transient cooling
notes.body:
Real problems rarely involve one mode of heat transfer on its own. Typical first-year exam questions combine conduction through a wall or casing with convection and radiation at its surfaces, or ask how quickly a small body heats up or cools down.

Resistance networks
- Series path: Q̇ = (T_hot − T_cold)/ΣR. Use R = L/(kA) for a plane layer, ln(r₂/r₁)/(2πkL) for a cylindrical layer and 1/(hA) for a convecting surface.
- Convection and radiation from the same surface to the same surroundings act in parallel. Add their coefficients: h_total = h_c + h_r.
- The overall heat transfer coefficient U is defined by Q̇ = UAΔT_overall, so 1/(UA) = ΣR. This is used for heat exchangers and walls.
- Once Q̇ is known, find any interface temperature by stepping through the resistances: T_next = T_previous − Q̇R.

Worked example (insulated pipe): a 100 mm diameter pipe with its surface at 150 °C is lagged to 160 mm diameter with insulation of k = 0.05 W/(m K). The air is at 20 °C and h = 10 W/(m² K).
- R_ins = ln(1.6)/(2π × 0.05) ≈ 1.496 K m/W.
- R_conv = 1/(10 × 2π × 0.08) ≈ 0.199 K m/W.
- Q̇ ≈ 130/1.695 ≈ 76.7 W per metre, and the outer surface is at about 20 + 76.7 × 0.199 ≈ 35 °C.
- The bare pipe would lose about 10 × 2π × 0.05 × 130 ≈ 408 W/m by convection alone, so the insulation cuts the loss by about 81%.

Critical radius of insulation
- Adding insulation to a small cylinder increases its outer surface area as well as its conduction resistance.
- For a cylinder, the heat loss is greatest when the outer radius equals r_c = k/h. For a sphere, r_c = 2k/h.
- If the bare radius is already at least r_c, any thickness of insulation reduces the heat loss. If the bare radius is below r_c, a thin layer increases the loss (it is greatest at r_c), and the insulation must be made much thicker before the loss falls below the bare value. With k = 0.05 and h = 10, r_c = 5 mm, so lagging the 50 mm radius pipe helps. For thin electrical wires the opposite holds, so a thin insulating sheath can help cool them.

Lumped-capacitance transient
- If the Biot number Bi = hL_c/k_solid is less than about 0.1, where L_c = V/A, the temperature inside the solid is nearly uniform.
- Then (T − T∞)/(T_i − T∞) = exp(−t/τ), with time constant τ = ρcV/(hA).
- Example: a 10 mm aluminium sphere (ρ = 2700 kg/m³, c = 900 J/(kg K), k = 200 W/(m K)) cooling in air with h = 50 W/(m² K).
- L_c = D/6 ≈ 1.67 mm, so Bi ≈ 4 × 10⁻⁴ and the lumped model applies.
- τ = 2700 × 900 × 0.00167/50 ≈ 81 s.
- Cooling from 300 °C to 50 °C in air at 25 °C takes t = 81 ln(275/25) ≈ 194 s.
- The same idea sets the response time of a thermocouple, which is a small bead with a low Biot number.

Exam tips: draw the network with every resistance labelled and its value written in, check whether radiation is significant (h_r is often 5–10 W/(m² K) near room temperature), and check Bi before using the lumped model.

cards.b: Q − W = ΔU (+ΔKE + ΔPE), with Q = heat added and W = work done by the system.

cards.f: Why enthalpy appears in flow problems
cards.b: Fluid entering or leaving a control volume carries u plus the flow work pv needed to push it across the boundary: u + pv = h.

cards.f: Combustor in the simple SFEE model
cards.b: No shaft work, so heat added per kg ≈ c_p(T₀₂ − T₀₁), ignoring the change in composition and in c_p.
ΔS = ∫δQ/T + S_gen, with S_gen ≥ 0. S_gen = 0 only for a reversible process.
Δs = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁). The same form holds with stagnation T₀ and p₀.

η_c = (T₀₂s − T₀₁)/(T₀₂ − T₀₁): ideal work ÷ actual work, both to the same exit pressure.
η_t = (T₀₁ − T₀₂)/(T₀₁ − T₀₂s): actual work ÷ ideal work, both to the same exit pressure.

cards.f: Entropy rise in an adiabatic duct
cards.b: With T₀ constant, Δs = −R ln(p₀₂/p₀₁), so any entropy generated shows up as a loss of stagnation pressure.
η = 1 − 1/r_p^((γ−1)/γ), which rises with the pressure ratio r_p.
a = √(γRT). For air at 288.15 K, a ≈ 340 m/s; at 216.65 K, a ≈ 295 m/s.
p*/p₀ = (2/(γ+1))^(γ/(γ−1)) ≈ 0.528 for γ = 1.4. The corresponding T*/T₀ = 0.833.
dA/A = (M² − 1) dV/V: subsonic flow accelerates in a converging duct, supersonic flow in a diverging duct, and M = 1 only at a throat.
When the throat reaches M = 1, the mass flow reaches its maximum for the given p₀ and T₀ and does not rise if the back pressure falls further.
ṁ ≈ 0.0404 A* p₀/√T₀ (SI units, γ = 1.4, R = 287 J/(kg K)).
M drops from supersonic to subsonic; p, T and ρ rise; T₀ stays constant; entropy rises, so p₀ falls.
q″ = −k dT/dx: conductive heat flux is proportional to the temperature gradient and flows from hot to cold.
R = L/(kA), so Q̇ = ΔT/R = kAΔT/L.
R = ln(r₂/r₁)/(2πkL) for a shell from inner radius r₁ to outer radius r₂, length L.
Series layers: add resistances (same Q̇ through each). Parallel paths: add conductances 1/R (same ΔT across each).
α = k/(ρc) (m²/s): how quickly a temperature change spreads through a material.
R_conv = 1/(hA), added in series with conduction resistances at a fluid–solid surface.

cards.f: Temperature profile in a plane wall vs a cylinder
cards.b: Steady 1D, constant k, no generation: linear in a plane wall, logarithmic in r for a cylindrical shell.
q″ = h(T_s − T∞). h depends on the flow, the fluid and the geometry; it is not a material property.
Nu = hL/k_f, using the fluid conductivity: the dimensionless convective heat transfer coefficient.
Pr = ν/α = c_pμ/k: momentum diffusivity ÷ thermal diffusivity. About 0.7 for air and roughly 5–7 for water at room temperature.
Re = VL/ν = ρVL/μ: inertial ÷ viscous forces. Flat-plate transition typically occurs at Re_x ≈ 5 × 10⁵.
Nu_L = 0.664 Re_L^(1/2) Pr^(1/3) (constant wall temperature, Pr ≳ 0.6). The local value is Nu_x = 0.332 Re_x^(1/2) Pr^(1/3).
Nu_D = 0.023 Re_D^0.8 Pr^n for fully developed turbulent pipe flow; n = 0.4 when heating the fluid, 0.3 when cooling it.
Buoyancy from density differences, measured by the Grashof number Gr = gβΔTL³/ν² (or Ra = Gr·Pr).
E_b = σT⁴, with σ ≈ 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/(m² K⁴) and T in kelvin.
λ_max T ≈ 2898 µm K. At 5800 K the peak is near 0.5 µm; at 300 K near 10 µm.
ε = emitted flux ÷ black-body flux at the same temperature (0 ≤ ε ≤ 1).
Spectral absorptivity equals spectral emissivity (α_λ = ε_λ) at thermal equilibrium. For a grey surface, α = ε overall.
Q̇ = εσA(T_s⁴ − T_sur⁴), with ε the emissivity of the small body.
A_iF_ij = A_jF_ji. In an enclosure the view factors from any surface sum to 1.
h_r = εσ(T_s + T_sur)(T_s² + T_sur²), so Q̇_rad = h_rA(T_s − T_sur).
q″ = σ(T₁⁴ − T₂⁴)/(1/ε₁ + 1/ε₂ − 1) for two large parallel grey diffuse plates.
U defined by Q̇ = UAΔT_overall, so 1/(UA) = ΣR along the heat path.

cards.f: Convection plus radiation at a surface
cards.b: They act in parallel between the surface and the surroundings: h_total = h_c + h_r.
r_c = k/h for a cylinder (2k/h for a sphere). For a bare cylinder smaller than r_c, a thin layer of insulation increases the heat loss (maximum at r_c).
Bi = hL_c/k_solid with L_c = V/A. If Bi < 0.1, the internal temperature is nearly uniform, so the lumped model applies.
(T − T∞)/(T_i − T∞) = exp(−t/τ), with τ = ρcV/(hA).
L_c = V/A = (πD³/6)/(πD²) = D/6.
Once Q̇ is known, step through: T_next = T_previous − Q̇ × R for each resistance in series.

questions.q: Which of these is a path function rather than a property?
questions.why: The heat transferred between two states depends on the process followed, so it is a path function. Enthalpy, entropy and pressure are properties: each has a single value at a given state, and its change depends only on the end states.

questions.q: What is the density of air (R = 287 J/(kg K)) at 101 325 Pa and 15 °C?
questions.why: ρ = p/(RT) = 101 325/(287 × 288.15) ≈ 1.23 kg/m³. Using 15 instead of 288.15 (Celsius, not kelvin) gives about 23.5 kg/m³. Entering the pressure as 101.325 kPa while keeping R in J/(kg K) is a factor of 1000 out, giving about 0.00123. Using the universal constant 8.314 J/(mol K) gives about 42.3, which is a molar concentration in mol/m³, not a density.

questions.q: An aircraft flies at 250 m/s where the static air temperature is 220 K and the static pressure is 0.3 bar. Taking c_p = 1005 J/(kg K) and γ = 1.4, find the stagnation temperature and the isentropic stagnation pressure.
questions.modelAnswer: Bringing the flow to rest adiabatically gives T₀ = T + V²/(2c_p) = 220 + 250²/(2 × 1005) = 220 + 31.1 ≈ 251.1 K. If the deceleration is also isentropic, p₀ = p(T₀/T)^(γ/(γ−1)) = 0.3 × (1.1413)^3.5 ≈ 0.3 × 1.588 ≈ 0.48 bar. This is the pressure an ideal (loss-free) intake would recover.

questions.q: An aircraft flies at 250 m/s in air at 220 K (c_p = 1005 J/(kg K), c_v = 718 J/(kg K)). What is the stagnation temperature?
questions.why: T₀ = T + V²/(2c_p) = 220 + 62 500/2010 ≈ 251 K. Dropping the factor of 2 (220 + 62 500/1005) gives about 282 K. Using c_v in place of c_p gives about 264 K, but the stagnation temperature comes from enthalpy, so c_p is the right specific heat. Leaving c_p in kJ/(kg K) while V² is in m²/s² gives about 31 300 K.

questions.q: Air at T₀₁ = 288 K is compressed through a pressure ratio of 10 (γ = 1.4, c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg K)) with an isentropic efficiency of 0.85. What is the specific work input?
questions.why: The isentropic temperature rise is 288(10^0.2857 − 1) ≈ 268 K, so the ideal work is about 269 kJ/kg. Dividing by 0.85 gives the actual work, about 317 kJ/kg. The value 269 kJ/kg ignores the efficiency. Multiplying by 0.85 instead of dividing gives about 229 kJ/kg, which would make the real compressor need less work than the ideal one. Using the exponent γ − 1 (that is, 10^0.4) treats 10 as a volume ratio and gives about 515 kJ/kg.

questions.q: Air leaves a combustor at T₀ = 1200 K and expands through an adiabatic convergent nozzle to an exit static temperature of 1000 K (c_p = 1148 J/(kg K) for the hot gas). Find the exit velocity. Then explain, using the SFEE, why the stagnation temperature is unchanged through the nozzle.
markScheme: SFEE with q = 0 and w = 0 gives h₀ constant, so T₀ constant (perfect gas) (2)
States that the assumptions are steady, adiabatic, no shaft work, negligible gravity (1)
questions.modelAnswer: Assume steady, adiabatic flow with no shaft work and negligible change in height. The SFEE then reduces to h₀₂ = h₀₁, and for a perfect gas with constant c_p this means T₀ is constant along the nozzle: the gas trades static enthalpy for kinetic energy without any change in total energy. The exit velocity follows from h₀ = h + V²/2: V = √(2c_p(T₀ − T)) = √(2 × 1148 × 200) = √459 200 ≈ 678 m/s.

questions.q: Air (c_p = 1.005, c_v = 0.718, R = 0.287 kJ/(kg K)) is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 600 K. What is its specific entropy change?
questions.why: At constant pressure the R ln(p₂/p₁) term vanishes, leaving Δs = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) = 1.005 × ln 2 ≈ 0.697 kJ/(kg K). Using c_v gives 0.498, but c_v belongs with the volume ratio form (constant volume). R ln 2 ≈ 0.199 uses the gas constant in place of c_p. 1.005 comes from c_p × ΔT/T₁, which treats the logarithm as linear.

questions.q: Gas at 1400 K expands through a turbine with pressure ratio 8. The isentropic exit temperature is 772.9 K and the actual exit temperature is 850 K. What is the turbine isentropic efficiency?
questions.why: η_t = (T₀₁ − T₀₂)/(T₀₁ − T₀₂s) = 550/627.1 ≈ 0.88. Using the compressor form (ideal ÷ actual) gives 627.1/550 ≈ 1.14, which is impossible for an efficiency. The ratio of exit temperatures, 772.9/850 ≈ 0.91, is not an efficiency definition. 1 − 772.9/1400 ≈ 0.45 is a Carnot-style ratio and not the component efficiency.

questions.q: Show that, for adiabatic flow of a perfect gas in a duct with no work, the specific entropy rise is Δs = −R ln(p₀₂/p₀₁). An intake recovers 97% of the free-stream stagnation pressure. Find Δs and comment.
markScheme: Starts from Δs = c_p ln(T₀₂/T₀₁) − R ln(p₀₂/p₀₁) (1)
Adiabatic, no work, so T₀₂ = T₀₁ and the first term vanishes (1)
Comment: positive, so the flow is irreversible; losses in an adiabatic duct appear as a fall in p₀ (1)
questions.modelAnswer: Apply the Gibbs relation between the two stagnation states: Δs = c_p ln(T₀₂/T₀₁) − R ln(p₀₂/p₀₁). With no heat and no work, the SFEE gives h₀₂ = h₀₁, so T₀₂ = T₀₁ and the first term is zero, leaving Δs = −R ln(p₀₂/p₀₁). For 97% recovery, Δs = −287 × ln 0.97 ≈ 287 × 0.03046 ≈ 8.74 J/(kg K). The positive value shows that friction and any shocks in the intake are irreversible. Since the duct is adiabatic, all of this entropy is generated inside it, and it appears as lost stagnation pressure.

questions.q: What is the speed of sound in air (γ = 1.4, R = 287 J/(kg K)) at 216.65 K?
questions.why: a = √(γRT) = √(1.4 × 287 × 216.65) ≈ 295 m/s. Leaving out γ gives √(RT) ≈ 249 m/s, which is the isothermal (Newton's) value. Using R in kJ/(kg K) gives about 9.3 m/s. 340 m/s is the sea-level value at 288 K; the speed of sound depends on temperature, so it is lower in the colder air at altitude.

questions.q: For air (γ = 1.4), what is the ratio of static pressure at a sonic throat to reservoir stagnation pressure, p*/p₀?
questions.why: p*/p₀ = (2/(γ+1))^(γ/(γ−1)) = (0.8333)^3.5 ≈ 0.528. The value 0.833 is T*/T₀ = 2/(γ+1), the temperature ratio. The value 0.634 is ρ*/ρ₀, which uses the exponent 1/(γ−1). 1.893 is the inverse ratio, p₀/p*.

questions.q: Air flows from a large reservoir at p₀ = 5 bar and T₀ = 500 K through a convergent nozzle with exit area 0.01 m² into surroundings at 1 bar. Show that the nozzle is choked, and find the exit static temperature, pressure, velocity and mass flow rate (γ = 1.4, R = 287 J/(kg K)).
markScheme: Critical back pressure 0.528 × 5 ≈ 2.64 bar > 1 bar, so choked, M_exit = 1 (1)
questions.modelAnswer: The critical pressure for this reservoir is 0.528 × 5 ≈ 2.64 bar. The back pressure of 1 bar is lower, so the nozzle is choked and the exit Mach number is 1. Exit temperature: T* = T₀/1.2 = 416.7 K. Exit pressure: p* ≈ 2.64 bar. The gas expands further outside the nozzle. Exit velocity: V* = √(1.4 × 287 × 416.7) ≈ 409 m/s. Density: ρ* = 2.641 × 10⁵/(287 × 416.7) ≈ 2.21 kg/m³. Mass flow: ṁ = 2.21 × 409 × 0.01 ≈ 9.04 kg/s, which matches 0.0404 × 0.01 × 5 × 10⁵/√500 ≈ 9.04 kg/s.

questions.q: A brick wall 0.2 m thick (k = 0.7 W/(m K)) has an area of 10 m² and a temperature difference of 20 K across it. What is the steady heat-transfer rate?
questions.why: Q̇ = kAΔT/L = 0.7 × 10 × 20/0.2 = 700 W. Entering the thickness as 20 (centimetres, not metres) gives 7 W. Multiplying by L instead of dividing gives 28 W. Leaving out the area gives 70, which is the heat flux in W/m², not the total rate.

questions.q: A wall has an inside convection coefficient of 10 W/(m² K), 0.2 m of brick (k = 0.7 W/(m K)), 0.05 m of insulation (k = 0.04 W/(m K)) and an outside coefficient of 25 W/(m² K). Inside air is at 20 °C and outside air at −5 °C. What is the heat flux?
questions.why: The four resistances per m² are in series: 0.1 + 0.286 + 1.25 + 0.04 ≈ 1.676 m² K/W, so q″ = 25/1.676 ≈ 14.9 W/m². Leaving out the insulation gives about 58.7 W/m². Leaving out the two convective resistances gives about 16.3 W/m². Adding the conductances as if the layers were in parallel gives about 982 W/m², but the heat must pass through every layer in turn.

questions.q: Derive the thermal resistance of a cylindrical shell of inner radius r₁, outer radius r₂, length L and conductivity k, starting from Fourier's law. Then find the heat loss per metre through pipe insulation with r₁ = 50 mm, r₂ = 80 mm, k = 0.05 W/(m K) and a 100 K difference across it.
markScheme: Q̇ = −k(2πrL) dT/dr, constant in steady state with no generation (1)
Separate and integrate: Q̇ ln(r₂/r₁) = 2πkL(T₁ − T₂) (1)
questions.modelAnswer: In steady state with no heat generation, the same Q̇ crosses every cylindrical surface of area 2πrL. Fourier's law gives Q̇ = −k(2πrL) dT/dr. Separating variables: Q̇ dr/r = −2πkL dT. Integrating from r₁ (T₁) to r₂ (T₂): Q̇ ln(r₂/r₁) = 2πkL(T₁ − T₂). So Q̇ = (T₁ − T₂)/R with R = ln(r₂/r₁)/(2πkL). For 1 m of insulation: R = ln(0.08/0.05)/(2π × 0.05 × 1) = 0.470/0.314 ≈ 1.496 K/W. The loss is Q̇ = 100/1.496 ≈ 66.8 W per metre.

questions.q: How is the Nusselt number defined?
options: hL/k, with k the thermal conductivity of the fluid
hL/k, with k the thermal conductivity of the solid
questions.why: Nu = hL/k_f compares convection with pure conduction through the fluid layer, so it uses the fluid's conductivity. The same expression with the solid's conductivity is the Biot number, which is used in transient conduction. ν/α is the Prandtl number, and ρVL/μ is the Reynolds number.

questions.q: Air (ν = 1.6 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s, k = 0.026 W/(m K), Pr = 0.71) flows at 5 m/s along a 0.5 m flat plate. Using Nu_L = 0.664 Re_L^(1/2) Pr^(1/3), what is the average heat transfer coefficient?
questions.why: Re_L ≈ 1.56 × 10⁵ (laminar), so Nu_L ≈ 0.664 × 395.3 × 0.892 ≈ 234 and h = Nu k/L ≈ 12.2 W/(m² K). Using the local coefficient 0.332 gives the value at the trailing edge, about 6.1, which is half the average. 234 is the Nusselt number itself, not yet converted to h. About 3.0 comes from multiplying by L instead of dividing (234 × 0.026 × 0.5).

questions.q: Water flows through a 20 mm diameter tube at Re_D = 50 000 and is being heated (Pr = 5, k = 0.6 W/(m K)). Using the Dittus–Boelter correlation, estimate h. State two conditions under which the correlation is valid.
markScheme: Conditions: fully developed turbulent flow (Re ≳ 10⁴), moderate Pr range (about 0.6–160), moderate wall–fluid temperature differences, long tube (1)
questions.modelAnswer: For a heated fluid, n = 0.4. Nu = 0.023 × 50 000^0.8 × 5^0.4 ≈ 0.023 × 5743 × 1.904 ≈ 251. Then h = Nu k/D = 251 × 0.6/0.02 ≈ 7 540 W/(m² K), or about 7.5 kW/(m² K). The correlation applies to fully developed turbulent flow (Re_D above about 10 000), Prandtl numbers between about 0.6 and 160, and tubes long compared with their diameter. It is less accurate when property variations across the flow are large.

questions.q: A small pipe surface at 400 K (ε = 0.8) is in a large room at 300 K. What is the net radiative heat flux from the pipe?
questions.why: q″ = εσ(T_s⁴ − T_sur⁴) = 0.8 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × (2.56 × 10¹⁰ − 8.1 × 10⁹) ≈ 794 W/m². Leaving out ε treats the pipe as black and gives about 992. Using 127 °C and 27 °C instead of kelvin gives about 11.8. Raising the temperature difference to the fourth power, εσ(ΔT)⁴, gives about 4.5; the law needs the difference of the fourth powers.

questions.q: Two large parallel plates at 600 K and 400 K both have ε = 0.8. What is the net radiative flux between them?
questions.why: q″ = σ(T₁⁴ − T₂⁴)/(1/ε₁ + 1/ε₂ − 1) = 5.90/(1.25 + 1.25 − 1) ≈ 3.93 kW/m². 5.90 kW/m² is the black-body value, ignoring both emissivities. Multiplying the black-body flux by ε₁ε₂ = 0.64 gives about 3.77, which ignores multiple reflections between the plates. Multiplying by a single ε = 0.8 gives about 4.72; that is the small-body-in-enclosure formula, which is the wrong geometry here.

questions.q: Explain why a spacecraft radiator panel is coated with a white paint of low solar absorptivity but high infrared emissivity, referring to Wien's law and Kirchhoff's law. Estimate the wavelength of peak emission for the panel at 300 K.
markScheme: Sunlight (source about 5800 K) peaks near 0.5 µm; the panel at 300 K emits near 2898/300 ≈ 9.7 µm (1)
Kirchhoff: α_λ = ε_λ at each wavelength, but the bands are different, so overall α_solar and ε_IR can differ (1)
Low α in the visible means little solar heat absorbed (1)
High ε in the infrared means strong emission of waste heat to space, which is the only rejection path (1)
questions.modelAnswer: From Wien's law, solar radiation (a source at about 5800 K) peaks near 0.5 µm, while a 300 K panel emits most strongly near 2898/300 ≈ 9.7 µm in the infrared. Kirchhoff's law links absorptivity and emissivity only at the same wavelength: α_λ = ε_λ. A surface can therefore absorb weakly in the visible (low solar absorptivity) while emitting strongly in the infrared (high emissivity). White paints behave like this. The panel picks up little heat from the Sun but radiates waste heat well, which matters because in vacuum there is no convection, so radiation is the only way to reject heat.

questions.q: When is the lumped-capacitance model valid for a cooling solid?
options: When Bi = hL_c/k_solid is below about 0.1, so temperature differences inside the solid are small
When Bi = hL_c/k_fluid is below about 0.1
When Bi is below about 0.1, because conduction inside the solid is then slow compared with surface convection
questions.why: A small Biot number means internal conduction resistance (L_c/k_solid) is tiny compared with surface convection resistance (1/h), so the solid stays nearly uniform in temperature. Using the fluid's conductivity gives a Nusselt-type group, not the Biot number. A Biot number above 10 means large internal gradients, the opposite of the lumped condition. The claim that internal conduction is slow at low Bi has the threshold right but the physics reversed: at low Bi internal conduction is fast, and it is the surface convection resistance that controls the cooling rate.

questions.q: A 10 mm aluminium sphere (ρ = 2700 kg/m³, c = 900 J/(kg K)) cools in air at 25 °C with h = 50 W/(m² K). How long does it take to cool from 300 °C to 50 °C?
questions.why: τ = ρcL_c/h with L_c = D/6, giving τ ≈ 81 s, and t = τ ln[(T_i − T∞)/(T − T∞)] = 81 ln(275/25) ≈ 194 s. 81 s is just the time constant; after one τ the excess temperature has fallen only to 37% of its initial value. Using the radius D/2 as L_c instead of V/A = D/6 gives about 583 s. Using ln(300/50), with temperatures instead of excess temperatures above the air, gives about 145 s.

questions.q: A surface at 350 K loses heat to still air at 300 K (h_c = 10 W/(m² K)) and to large surroundings at 300 K. Its emissivity is 0.9. Estimate the radiation coefficient h_r, the total heat flux, and the percentage of the loss due to radiation.
questions.modelAnswer: Radiation coefficient: h_r = εσ(T_s + T_sur)(T_s² + T_sur²) = 0.9 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 650 × (122 500 + 90 000) ≈ 7.05 W/(m² K). Convection and radiation act in parallel between the same temperatures, so q″ = (10 + 7.05) × 50 ≈ 852 W/m². Radiation provides 7.05/17.05 ≈ 41% of the loss. Ignoring it would underestimate the heat loss badly even at this modest temperature.

questions.q:
Air (γ = 1.4, R = 287 J/(kg K), c_p = 1005 J/(kg K)) is supplied from a large reservoir at p₀ = 5 bar and T₀ = 500 K to a nozzle with a throat area of 0.01 m².
(a) Define stagnation temperature and pressure, and show from the SFEE that T₀ is constant in adiabatic flow with no work. [4]
(b) The nozzle is convergent and discharges to 1 bar. Show that it is choked and find the exit velocity and the mass flow rate. [6]
(c) The back pressure is raised to 4 bar. Find the exit Mach number, velocity and mass flow rate. [5]
(d) A divergent section is added so the flow expands isentropically to M = 2 at the exit. Find the exit-to-throat area ratio and the exit static pressure. A normal shock now stands at the exit plane. Give the Mach number behind it and the fraction of stagnation pressure retained. [5]
markScheme: (a) Definitions; SFEE with q = w = 0 gives h + V²/2 constant, so T₀ = T + V²/(2c_p) is constant (4)
(b) 0.528 × 5 = 2.64 bar > 1 bar so choked, M = 1 at exit; T* = 416.7 K, V* ≈ 409 m/s (3)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The stagnation temperature T₀ and pressure p₀ are the values the gas would reach if brought to rest: adiabatically for T₀, and isentropically for p₀. For steady flow with no heat or work and negligible height change, the SFEE gives h₁ + V₁²/2 = h₂ + V₂²/2, so h₀ = h + V²/2 is constant. For a perfect gas with constant c_p, h = c_pT, so T₀ = T + V²/(2c_p) is constant along the nozzle. p₀ is also constant only if the flow is isentropic.

(b) The critical pressure is p* = 0.528 × 5 ≈ 2.64 bar. The back pressure of 1 bar is lower, so the throat (the exit of a convergent nozzle) is sonic and the flow is choked. T* = T₀/1.2 = 416.7 K and V* = √(1.4 × 287 × 416.7) ≈ 409 m/s. ρ* = 2.641 × 10⁵/(287 × 416.7) ≈ 2.21 kg/m³, so ṁ = ρ*V*A ≈ 2.21 × 409 × 0.01 ≈ 9.04 kg/s. This agrees with 0.0404Ap₀/√T₀ = 0.0404 × 0.01 × 5 × 10⁵/22.36 ≈ 9.04 kg/s.

(c) With 4 bar above the critical pressure, the exit is subsonic and its pressure equals the back pressure. Then p₀/p = 1.25, so 1 + 0.2M² = 1.25^(1/3.5) = 1.0658, giving M ≈ 0.574. T = 500/1.0658 ≈ 469.1 K, a = √(1.4 × 287 × 469.1) ≈ 434 m/s, and V ≈ 0.574 × 434 ≈ 249 m/s. ρ = 4 × 10⁵/(287 × 469.1) ≈ 2.97 kg/m³, so ṁ ≈ 2.97 × 249 × 0.01 ≈ 7.40 kg/s, which is below the choked value.

(d) A/A* = (1/M)[(2/2.4)(1 + 0.2M²)]³ = 0.5 × (0.8333 × 1.8)³ = 0.5 × 1.5³ = 1.6875, so the exit area is about 0.0169 m². The exit static pressure is p_e = 5/(1 + 0.2 × 4)^3.5 = 5/7.82 ≈ 0.639 bar, and T_e = 500/1.8 ≈ 277.8 K. Across a normal shock at M₁ = 2: M₂² = (1 + 0.2 × 4)/(1.4 × 4 − 0.2) = 1.8/5.4 = 1/3, so M₂ ≈ 0.577. The static pressure rises by p₂/p₁ = 1 + (2.8/2.4)(4 − 1) = 4.5, to about 2.88 bar. The stagnation-pressure ratio is p₀₂/p₀₁ ≈ 0.721, so about 28% of the stagnation pressure is lost because of the entropy rise across the shock. T₀ is unchanged.

questions.q:
A steam pipe with outer radius 50 mm has its outer surface at 150 °C. It runs through a hangar where the air and surroundings are at 20 °C. The convective coefficient on any outer surface is 10 W/(m² K).
(a) For the bare pipe, find the heat loss per metre by convection alone. Then estimate the radiative loss if the bare surface has ε = 0.9. [5]
(b) The pipe is lagged with insulation (k = 0.05 W/(m K)) to an outer radius of 80 mm. Ignoring radiation, draw the resistance network and find the heat loss per metre and the outer surface temperature. [7]
(c) Find the critical radius of insulation and explain whether adding this lagging was worthwhile. [4]
(d) Explain qualitatively how including radiation from the lagged surface (ε = 0.9) would change your answers to (b). [4]
markScheme: (c) r_c = k/h = 5 mm < 50 mm, so insulation reduces loss; loss cut by about 81% (convection basis) (4)

(d) Radiation adds a parallel resistance at the outer surface, lowering the outer resistance; Q̇ rises slightly (to about 80 W/m) and the surface temperature falls (to about 30 °C); the insulation still dominates (4)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Bare pipe, per metre: the convective loss is Q̇ = h(2πr₁L)(T_s − T∞) = 10 × 0.3142 × 130 ≈ 408 W/m. The radiative loss is Q̇ = εσA(T_s⁴ − T_sur⁴) = 0.9 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 0.3142 × (423.15⁴ − 293.15⁴). The fourth powers are about 3.206 × 10¹⁰ and 0.738 × 10¹⁰, a difference of about 2.468 × 10¹⁰, so Q̇_rad ≈ 396 W/m. (Equivalently, h_r ≈ 9.7 W/(m² K).) Radiation roughly doubles the bare-pipe loss, to about 800 W/m.

(b) The network is two resistances in series between 150 °C and 20 °C: insulation, then outer convection. R_ins = ln(80/50)/(2π × 0.05 × 1) = 0.4700/0.3142 ≈ 1.496 K/W per metre. R_conv = 1/(h × 2πr₂) = 1/(10 × 0.5027) ≈ 0.199 K/W per metre. The total is about 1.695 K/W, so Q̇ = 130/1.695 ≈ 76.7 W/m. The outer surface temperature is T₂ = 20 + 76.7 × 0.199 ≈ 35.3 °C.

(c) For a cylinder, r_c = k/h = 0.05/10 = 0.005 m = 5 mm. The pipe radius of 50 mm is already ten times r_c, so any added insulation raises the total resistance and reduces the loss. Compared with convection alone, the loss falls from about 408 to 77 W/m, a cut of about 81%. Including radiation from the bare pipe, the cut is larger still, about 90%. The lagging is clearly worthwhile; it also keeps the surface at a temperature that is safe to touch.

(d) Radiation from the lagged surface to the surroundings acts in parallel with convection, so the outer resistance becomes 1/((h_c + h_r)2πr₂). At around 30–35 °C, h_r is about 5.4 W/(m² K), which lowers the outer resistance from about 0.199 to about 0.129 K/W per metre. Because the insulation resistance (about 1.5 K/W per metre) dominates, the heat loss rises only a little, to about 80 W/m, while the surface temperature falls to about 30 °C. This needs an iteration, because h_r depends on the surface temperature. The conclusion in (c) is unchanged.
